extracted.intended_audience: observational astronomers and scientifically literate readers interested in Mars
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and interpretive rules for observing, measuring, and explaining the behavior of Mars' polar caps from telescopic/photographic data, with attention to seasonal changes, viewing geometry, and surface vs atmospheric causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of polar-cap size (use of longitude/latitude extents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine cap dimensions by recording its extent in longitude and latitude at times of observation, accounting for apparent foreshortening and pole tilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report diameters inferred from longitudinal/latitudinal endpoints and compare measures across oppositions; account for horizonward foreshortening and pole tilt when converting apparent extents to true diameters. Example measures: in 1903 and 1905 determinations implied diameters of ~96–97° (accounting for tilt and foreshortening). Use consensus of multiple measures to reduce error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark border as indicator of melting
rubrics_metrics.description: A dark line bordering a polar cap demonstrates that melting has set in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cap is 'bordered by a dark line', interpret that as evidence of active melting; absence of such a dark contour suggests the cap has not yet begun to melt (example: southern cap without dark contour in 1903 and 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indistinct edge diagnosis (depositing vs early melting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vague, ill‑defined cap edge indicates either ongoing deposition (still growing) or incipient melting/evaporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ambiguity of outline to infer stage: if frost is still depositing the edge will be indefinite; if melting/evaporation has just begun the edge will also be undefined until melt-water gathers. Do not assign a precise turning-point date when outline is wavering—it may be physically impossible to fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing surface deposit from cloud (canal visibility test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If underlying dark markings (canals) remain visible through a white area, the whiteness is surface frost/hoarfrost rather than suspended cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When canals or dark features can be traced through the white stretch, interpret the white as a surface deposit rather than atmospheric cloud. Example: deposition patches in 1903 allowed canal lines (Pierius, Enipeus) to be seen through the white, proving it was surface frost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency and fixed location of rifts implies surface origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Rifts that recur in the same positions year after year indicate dependence on local surface features rather than transient atmospheric phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record rift positions across oppositions; consistent recurrence in the same locations supports interpreting them as features tied to the surface (not ephemeral weather). Example: rifts seen in 1884 and 1897 reappeared in the same positions in 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rifts and beads originate from melt-product accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rifts typically arise from broader 'beads' in the dark blue belt encircling the cap—spots where melt-product is collected or most visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rifts start from bead-like broadenings of the encircling dark belt, interpret these as loci of concentrated melt or runoff that produce penetrating dark rifts into the cap; such rifts may traverse and split the cap into detachable patches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altitude/elevation is negligible as an explanatory factor on Mars
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Mars has low gravity and thus a more rapidly rarefying atmosphere with altitude, modest topographic relief cannot produce the temperature differentials needed to explain local melting patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invoking elevation/depression as causes for local melting or rifts unless elevation differences are implausibly large; the book argues Mars lacks elevations over ~2–3 thousand feet and gravity (≈3/8 Earth's) makes altitude effects three times less influential than on Earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring haze (hood of vapor) as evidence of in-situ evaporation/condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: An indistinct, enlarged-looking cap edge or 'hood' of different dull white indicates vapor condensed from excessive local evaporation—i.e., steaming in situ rather than a wafted cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a cap about 25° diameter becomes hazy and appears to grow in apparent size, interpret this as a veil of vapor formed by intense melting and local condensation; the veil tends to appear in mid‑spring (example: May 15) and later dissipates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minima are easier to measure than maxima due to viewing geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the planet's axial tilt and vantage from Earth, caps at their minima are often better presented for measurement than at their maxima, making minima more accurately known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that hemisphere tilt toward the Sun (summer) both reduces cap extent and presents it more directly to observers, while maxima often occur when the pole is tilted away and foreshortened. Use this geometric understanding when weighing data quality (e.g., northern cap minimum ≈6°, southern ≈5°; south vanished in 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Season length and daily intensity affect maxima and minima differently
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the season (determined by orbital eccentricity) governs accumulation during winter (maxima), while the intensity and continuity of heat during summer (few very hot days) disproportionately govern melting (minima).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For maxima: longer, colder winters add more daily accumulation—e.g., a longer antarctic night leads to a larger southern maximum. For minima: a shorter season with more intense daily heat can melt more effectively, because surplus heat above melting point, persistence of warm conditions, and formation of humid air blankets amplify melting beyond total insolation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glaciation requires both favorable eccentricity and large precipitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eccentricity alone does not produce universal glaciation; a combination of favorable orbital circumstances and high precipitation is required to form sustained ice-sheets (ice ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or explaining glaciation, include both factors: eccentricity that concentrates insolation seasonally and an increased vapor/precipitation budget that locks deposits into growing depth rather than mere extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrounding surface character influences cap behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and color of regions surrounding a cap (e.g., blue‑green areas versus ochre) affect melting/evaporation behavior and thus cap dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare environmental context around each pole when interpreting differences: the southern cap's surroundings of blue‑green areas (sometimes extending near equator) versus the northern cap's continuous ochre may explain differing melt/evaporation patterns and the presence or absence of spring haze.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended temporal coverage (observe beyond opposition) is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: To capture the full seasonal career of the caps (onset, maximum, melting, re-formation), observations must be extended well before and after opposition rather than limited to the time near closest approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin observations up to four months before opposition and continue as long after as possible; extended coverage allowed discovery of seasonal phenomena (e.g., earliest recorded cap starts, bridging of previous chronology gaps between Feb 25 and April 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transient appearance (fission into patches) should be interpreted as progressive melting
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cap develops dark rifts that cleave it into separate subsidiary patches which then dwindle, interpret this as stages of progressive melting rather than permanent reconfiguration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track the lifecycle of detached patches: rifts penetrate from periphery, traverse the cap, produce outlying patches that decrease and disappear. Reappearance or persistence of certain patches across years can indicate more persistent local conditions but temporary detachments are signs of seasonal melt.
